news_headline: Google Loses EU Court Appeal Over €4.1 Billion Android Antitrust Fine
post_text:
On July 2, Europe's top court permanently closed Google's final appeal against a €4.1 billion ($4.7B) antitrust fine, first levied by the European Commission in 2018 for forcing smartphone makers to pre-install Google Search and Chrome as mandatory defaults on Android devices. The European Court of Justice ruling is unappealable, and under the EU Antitrust Damages Directive, it now functions as binding proof of violation in follow-on civil suits across 13 European nations, meaning rival companies can pursue additional damages without having to re-litigate whether Google broke the law.

The fine itself is almost secondary at this point. What the ruling cements is the EU's theory of harm: that bundling your own apps into a dominant platform is anticompetitive on its face, regardless of whether consumer prices went up. That argument, once seen as aggressive, is now settled law in the world's largest trading bloc. The Digital Markets Act piles on further, requiring Google to open Android to rival AI assistants and share data with competitors.

WBR's piece on the war against Big Tech mapped exactly this arc, antitrust regulators shifting their target from price effects to structural dominance, with Google, Apple, Amazon, and Meta all in the crosshairs. The ECJ ruling is that thesis playing out to its conclusion. Worth reading alongside the news.

#BigTech #Antitrust
